question: Why is it important to use a methodology for project management? Identify the main methodologies that could be used. Pick THREE and explain the advantages and disadvantages of each, and the types of project they suit. (20 marks)
hints: Start with structure, consistent working practices, clear responsibilities, coordination and control. Explain the benefit; using a named method alone does not guarantee success.
Compare three approaches consistently: what it does, a suitable project, at least one benefit, at least one limitation, and a reasoned judgement.
Waterfall uses sequential delivery and can suit relatively stable requirements, including parts of construction. It supports planning but later changes may be expensive.

Agile is an umbrella of values and approaches; Scrum is a framework using Sprints and feedback. These can suit evolving software work but require active collaboration. A fixed budget can be set while scope is prioritised.

PRINCE2 provides governance, responsibilities and stage decisions. It can support public-sector or other projects at different scales; documentation should be tailored rather than automatically heavy.
PMBOK is a guide to a body of knowledge, not one delivery methodology. Kanban manages flow; Lean addresses waste and Six Sigma addresses process variation. Explain these distinctions if naming them.

question: Explain what project scope management is and why it is important for effective project management. Identify and explain the methods used to manage project scope, giving examples. Finally, explain how change management links to project scope. (20 marks)
hints: Define what the project includes and excludes. Link scope control to agreed needs and deliverables.

Explain the charter, scope statement, deliverables, exclusions, measurable acceptance criteria and work breakdown structure. Scope validation concerns acceptance; control concerns monitoring and managing changes.
Use one example: adding a payment feature to a booking app changes the agreed requirements and needs assessment.
Assess possible effects on time, cost, quality, benefits and risk. Do not assume every change necessarily alters all of them.

For the course PRINCE2 terminology, distinguish a request for change, off-specification and problem/concern. Explain capture, examine, propose, decide and implement, with the appropriate Change Authority and funding.
Evaluate how clear baselines and authorised decisions limit scope creep while allowing useful changes.

question: What are the seven themes of the PRINCE2 methodology and what do they involve? Apply these themes to an IT project and give examples of how they help manage it effectively. (20 marks)
hints: Use the older course themes: Business Case, Organisation, Quality, Plans, Risk, Change and Progress. Do not substitute principles or processes.
Business Case asks why the investment remains worthwhile. Organisation defines who represents business, user and supplier interests and who directs, manages and delivers.
Quality establishes expectations, criteria and checks. Plans link products, activities, resources, time and cost at suitable levels.
Risk addresses uncertainty. Change controls issues and alterations to baselines. Progress compares actual and forecast performance against agreed controls.
Apply all seven to the same IT project: justification for a new system; named roles; acceptance tests; migration plan; data-loss risk; controlled feature requests; and reports to the board.
The supplied notes suggest emphasis on explaining all seven and applying examples. Use the actual exam mark allocation when provided.

question: What are the seven principles of PRINCE2 and what do they involve? Give examples of how these principles help manage a business project effectively. (20 marks)
hints: Use the course wording: continued business justification; learn from experience; defined roles and responsibilities; manage by stages; manage by exception; focus on products; tailor to suit the project.
Explain each requirement and connect it to an action. A named document alone is not evidence that a principle has been followed.
For a music festival, review whether ticket demand still justifies costs, apply lessons from earlier events and assign sponsor, user and supplier responsibilities.
Agree management-stage decisions and tolerances. Define products such as a safe venue and approved programme before scheduling activities.
Tailor reporting and documentation to size and risk. Explain the downside of neglecting the principles, such as unclear decisions or continuing after the benefit has disappeared.
The terms universal, self-validating and empowering describe the principles in the supplied study notes; explain their practical meaning rather than listing the labels alone.

question: Identify the three categories of PRINCE2 management products. Explain what each involves and give examples of how they are used. Alternative question: explain the seven PRINCE2 processes. (20 marks)
hints: For the management-products version, organise the answer into baselines, records and reports.
Baselines are approved reference information under change control, such as the Business Case, PID, plans and Product Descriptions.
Records develop as the project runs: Daily Log, Risk Register, Issue Register, Quality Register and Lessons Log. Explain how they support decisions.
Reports provide information at a point in time: Checkpoint, Highlight, End Stage, Exception and End Project Reports. State who prepares and receives relevant reports.

Only if asked the alternative, explain Starting up a Project, Directing a Project, Initiating a Project, Controlling a Stage, Managing Product Delivery, Managing a Stage Boundary and Closing a Project.

Directing spans the lifecycle and delivery processes interact; do not present all seven as one simple linear sequence. Use the class Luton case only where its actual details are available, or label another example as hypothetical.

question: What is your understanding of risk management? What techniques can be used to identify and monitor risk in a project? Using examples, explain how risk should be communicated to different types of stakeholders. (20 marks)
hints: Define uncertainty affecting objectives, including threats and opportunities. Distinguish a possible event from a problem already occurring.
Identify using brainstorming, mind maps, interviews, nominal group technique and Delphi. Explain how a technique would uncover a risk.

A risk breakdown structure organises sources. A probability-impact grid helps assessment and prioritisation. Monitoring also requires owners, response actions, triggers, status and reviews in the risk register.
Illustrate proportionate responses: avoid, reduce, transfer, accept, share and, where appropriate in the course terminology, fallback. Opportunities require suitable opportunity responses.

Tailor communication: board-level exposure and decisions; relevant tasks and triggers for delivery staff; practical plain-language updates for affected users. Access to the full register depends on role and confidentiality.

The photographed risk question uses 2 marks for definition, 4 for identification, 4 for monitoring and 10 for stakeholder communication. Apply that split only when it matches the question and guidance you receive.

question: Explain what project screening is and why it is important. Identify the types of models used to screen project ideas. Pick TWO models and evaluate the benefits of using them, with examples. (20 marks)
hints: Explain how screening directs limited resources towards feasible and strategically useful proposals.
Distinguish non-numerical approaches, such as strategic or operating necessity, from numerical approaches, such as weighted scores, payback and NPV.
An unscored checklist can be qualitative; a checklist with assigned scores is numerical. Do not assume every checklist gives criteria equal importance unless that is how it is designed.
For weighted scoring, compare candidate IT tools using agreed criteria and weights. Benefits include transparency and non-financial criteria; subjectivity and sensitivity to weights are limitations.
NPV discounts future cash flows and subtracts the investment. It reflects timing and value but depends on forecast quality. State assumptions for any example.
The photographed screening guidance allocates 4 marks to explanation, 4 to identifying models and 12 to two models with examples and at least two benefits each. Include limitations for evaluation.

question: Explain what tools and techniques can be used to schedule a project effectively, giving examples. Pick TWO techniques and evaluate the benefits of using them. (20 marks)
hints: Identify the contribution of a WBS, dependency network, critical path analysis, Gantt chart, PERT and resource levelling. A WBS structures scope; it does not establish a schedule by itself.
A Gantt chart communicates dates and overlaps and supports progress tracking. Large charts can obscure dependencies unless links are maintained.

Critical path analysis identifies the dependency path controlling the planned duration. Under standard unconstrained scheduling assumptions, critical tasks have zero total float. Resource limits or imposed dates can complicate this.
PERT uses expected duration = (optimistic + 4 × most likely + pessimistic) ÷ 6. Explain the assumptions and why estimates remain uncertain.
Resource levelling adjusts work to available capacity and may change completion dates. Use an example such as competing festival setup tasks sharing the same crew.
For the two selected techniques, explain at least two useful benefits, limitations and a practical decision. Treat the supplied 12/8 split as a study suggestion unless confirmed by the exam paper.

question: Identify the main stakeholders of a project, giving examples. Explain why stakeholder analysis is important and how it can be done. Finally, explain how the analysis affects interaction with these stakeholders, with examples. (20 marks)
hints: Define stakeholders as people or groups who can affect, or are affected by, the project.
Identify internal and external interests: sponsor, team, managers, users, suppliers, regulators and local residents. Explain discovery through discussion, interviews or other appropriate methods.
Use a stakeholder register and power-interest analysis to prioritise engagement. Assess current and desired engagement; reassess as interests and influence change.
Apply the power-interest responses: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed and monitor. Explain actual information, channel, frequency and responsibility.
For a festival, contrast sponsor financial decisions, supplier delivery coordination, council licensing requirements and resident noise information.
The supplied study split is 7/7/6 across identification, analysis and interaction. It is not a confirmed allocation for a future exam.

question: Explain what is meant by project quality management and the different ways quality can be monitored and controlled, using specific examples. (20 marks)
hints: Define quality in relation to fitness for use and agreed requirements. Explain how poor quality can create rework, delays and dissatisfaction.
Distinguish planning quality, assurance of suitable processes and control through checking products. PRINCE2 Project Assurance and organisational quality assurance are not identical roles.
Explain at least three methods with examples: inspection/testing, structured quality reviews, fishbone investigation, Pareto analysis or control charts.
For an app, test specified behaviour and accessibility; use fishbone analysis to investigate recurring failures; use a Pareto chart to prioritise recorded defect types.

Connect quality expectations to measurable acceptance criteria and responsible producers, reviewers and approvers. MoSCoW prioritises requirements; it does not itself define whether a requirement passes an acceptance test.
Evaluate data quality, suitability of each tool and retesting after correction. The supplied 5/15 split is indicative study guidance, not a guaranteed future allocation.

question: Explain why cost estimation is an important part of project budgeting. Identify and explain at least THREE ways costs can be estimated, and explain how costs can be controlled. (20 marks)
hints: Connect credible estimates to affordability, the Business Case and decisions about resources. Explain uncertainty rather than presenting estimates as guarantees.

Compare at least three methods, for example analogous/top-down estimation, bottom-up estimation and parametric estimation. If using activity-based costing, explain how activities consume resources and distinguish it from a complete forecasting method.

Use the course labels ballpark, comparative, feasibility and definitive where required, but do not treat the supplied ±30%, ±10% and ±5% ranges as universal standards. Ranges depend on maturity, sector and agreed estimating practice.
Compare like-for-like budget and actual spending, investigate differences and manage changes. A simple spending variance is not the same as earned-value cost variance.

Earned value: PV = planned value (BCWS); EV = earned value (BCWP); AC = actual cost (ACWP). CV = EV − AC; SV = EV − PV; CPI = EV ÷ AC; SPI = EV ÷ PV. CPI below 1 means poorer cost efficiency than planned; SPI below 1 indicates less earned progress than planned.
Example: PV £10,000, EV £8,000, AC £12,000 gives CV −£4,000, SV −£2,000, CPI 0.67 and SPI 0.80. Investigate causes and update forecasts; a contingency fund does not remove approval requirements.

question: Effective project governance is linked to project success. Explain what project governance involves and the different roles and structure of governance, using a specific project example. (20 marks)
hints: Define the framework for decision authority, accountability, oversight and control. Distinguish governing from managing daily work.
Explain approval gates, reporting, risk/issue escalation, assurance and continued justification.
Distinguish sponsor, Project Board or steering committee, PMO and Project Manager. A PMO supports governance in ways defined by the organisation; it does not automatically replace the board.
Apply the roles to an IT project: sponsor owns investment rationale, board authorises stages within authority, manager coordinates delivery and assurance provides appropriate independent scrutiny.
If using Crossrail, HS2 or the Channel Tunnel, verify any dates, costs and outcome claims from credible sources. Naming a famous project alone is not application.
Evaluate the risks of excessive intervention, unclear authority or absent oversight. The supplied 4/4/8/4 mark split is a study suggestion unless confirmed for the question.
